#5842. Another Surgical Treatment for Back Pain Fails in Rigorous Analysis

— Norwegian registry data show no benefit from spine fusion as part of decompression surgery

Spinal fusion added to decompression surgery in patients with spinal stenosis did not provide any added benefit versus decompression alone, Norwegian national registry data indicated.

With outcomes compared for 1,446 patients undergoing decompression alone and 806 having spinal fusion as well, no significant difference in Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) scores was seen a year later, according to James H. McAuley, PhD, of Neuroscience Research Australia in Randwick, and colleagues.

This is not the first study to question the utility of spinal fusion for patients with degenerative stenosis, the group noted in their report appearing in Annals of Internal Medicine. Earlier, prospective trials in Sweden and Norway found no improvement in disability when compared with decompression surgery alone, as did a smaller U.S.-based study (although the latter did show better quality of life with fusion). Moreover, these trials all showed a higher burden of complications such as bleeding with spinal fusion, along with prolonged operative time and increased costs.

Nevertheless, McAuley and colleagues observed, including fusion in decompression procedures is now common practice in some countries, particularly the U.S. and Australia. One analysis in 2023 found that fully 90% of U.S. surgeries for degenerative spondylolisthesis in 2019 involved spine fusion -- a 23-point increase from just 3 years previously. McAuley's group had no explanation for this explosion in popularity, while the authors of the 2023 analysis pointed to "financial incentives, lack of guidelines and/or national regulations, and delayed evidence dissemination through medical education or professional societies."

Degenerative spondylolisthesis is a common feature of spinal stenosis; it involves a forward shift in a vertebra relative to those below it. Some surgeons have viewed this as indicative of instability that should be rectified via fusion, which seems plausible on its face but, as noted above, rigorous evidence for actual benefit is weak at best.

The current study sought to extend the findings from that Norwegian trial, called NORDSTEN-DS, by examining spinal stenosis patients' outcomes as recorded in the country's national health registry. They identified a total of some 3,900 patients undergoing surgery for degenerative spondylolisthesis from 2007 to 2021. NORDSTEN-DS participants' data were included in the registry and analyzed anew in the current study, which used a "target trial emulation" approach to compare patients undergoing versus not having fusion as part of decompression surgery. After excluding patients who, for example, were very elderly or had previous surgeries in the same spinal region, the investigators had 2,252 patients for detailed analysis, including 236 who were in NORDSTEN-DS.

Mean patient age was about 65 and roughly 70% were women. ODI scores at the time of surgery averaged 38.9 for those having decompression alone and 41.4 for the group undergoing fusion (higher scores indicate worse symptoms, and the maximum is 50).

At month 12 after surgery, mean ODI scores declined to 20.0 for the fusion group and 22.3 among those undergoing decompression alone. The mean difference of 2.2 points fell short of statistical significance (95% CI -1.6 to 6.1).

McAuley and colleagues also performed some subgroup analyses to see whether patients who would be more likely to benefit from fusion could be identified from baseline characteristics, such as age, sex, body mass index, or symptom severity. This effort came up empty, as no significant differences in ODI improvement emerged. However, it did show that men with obesity (BMI ≥30) had significantly worse outcomes versus men with lower BMI values.

And, as with earlier studies, fusion led to longer operative time (mean 85 extra minutes) and longer hospital stays (mean 1.9 extra days) compared with decompression alone. Although no particular complication stood out as more common with fusion, the risk for any type of complication was doubled overall. Risk for needing additional surgery because of complications was increased even more.

"This study calls into question the highly prevalent management of pain from lumbar degenerative spondylolisthesis with fusion," McAuley and colleagues wrote. "Our findings add to current evidence and should prompt reevaluation of current guidelines," which, they noted, are sparse and "offer conflicting recommendations."

Limitations to the study included the reliance on administrative records, the potential for confounding by unmeasured variables, and the 12-month window for examining outcomes, leaving open the possibility that fusion could have longer-term benefits.

#5841. Turtle Wax Is Concerned About Your Love Life, And Claims Messy Cars Impact Dating

Dating today can be "a nightmare of confusion and poor outcomes," according to Psychology Today, but don't worry, Jalopnik and Turtle Wax are on the case. We've already checked in with readers to see which cars to avoid on a first date, along with which ones instantly tell you their owners have good taste. Now, thanks to a survey recently commissioned by the Turtle Wax team, we can go a little deeper: If you really want to make a good impression the next time you take someone out, first take the time to clean up your car.

The survey, conducted by Talker Research on behalf of Turtle Wax, looked at what people thought about potential partners' car-care routines. For instance, out of the 2,000 "actively dating Americans" questioned, 73% said the way people take care of their cars and the way they take care of themselves go hand in hand. Moreover, 67% of those surveyed responded that they can tell if people have messy personal lives by looking at how messy their vehicles are. Coming at it from the other angle, 65% of the survey respondents agreed that a clean, well-ordered vehicle is a sign someone has a clean, well-ordered life.

In fact, 25% of the folks surveyed said they've ended a date early because the driver's car was dirty. The real surprise is that that number wasn't any higher. After all, some of the disgusting items survey-takers had seen in cars included at least one box with a dead cat in it, live roaches and maggots, bottles of urine, moldy milk, and that all-time classic, used condoms.

Driving a messy car can affect more than just your chance for romance. Working our way from the outside in, one welcome benefit of a clean exterior is that it can improve your vehicle's fuel economy — if the car starts out dirty enough, it can see a fuel-efficiency gain approaching 10% once it's been cleaned. And every percentage point counts, given today's fuel prices.

Some road filth can actively damage your car as well. Tree sap and bird poop are prime examples: They can eat right through your vehicle's exterior finish if you don't clean them up promptly. It's a similar story with road salt and other corrosives, which can cause a car to rust if not regularly washed off. Either way, the result can be a cascade of problems. Keep the car, and you could face costly repairs. Try to sell it, and you're likely to get less for a cruddy-looking vehicle than for one that's been freshly detailed. Meanwhile, leaving grime and dust on your windows can turn into a major safety issue if they limit your visibility.

Getting into a car with a disgusting interior can open up its own set of issues. One of the worst is if you drop food or drinks in the cabin and simply leave the spill laying there. Then mold can start forming in your car. Oh, and remember the dead cat in a box mentioned above? Yeah, driving around with dead animals is another bad idea, since they can carry salmonella, hantavirus, e. coli, and more.

#5840. Participation in Sunrun’s Puerto Rico VPP program doubled in 2026

Sunrun announced that participation in its Puerto Rico distributed power plant has doubled to more than 60,000 customers, representing nearly 70,000 home batteries. The distributed power plant frequently and reliably delivers 45 MW of dispatchable power for four hours at a time, providing critical support to Puerto Rico’s electric grid.

Since April, Sunrun has dispatched its power plant more than 60 times to weather severe energy shortfalls and prevent rolling blackouts. During an extended period of unseasonably hot temperatures this fall, Sunrun dispatched its home batteries to the grid for 18 consecutive days beginning October 13.

Sunrun’s Puerto Rico distributed power plant has scaled rapidly since 2024, when approximately 4,000 customers were enrolled. Enrollment surged to more than 30,000 customers in 2025. Sunrun is the largest aggregator in Puerto Rico’s Customer Battery Energy Sharing program.

Puerto Rico’s electric utility operator, LUMA, said in June and again in July that energy from home batteries helped “maintain system stability and prevent outages that would have affected thousands of customers.”

“What began in Puerto Rico out of necessity for family resilience has become a vital blueprint for the U.S. mainland, where severe weather and the proliferation of AI data centers are demanding new energy solutions,” said Sunrun CEO Mary Powell. “Sunrun is uniquely positioned to provide these solutions, whether to support a grid at its breaking point or to provide capacity for hyperscalers looking to come online.”

Sunrun’s increased dispatching capacity in Puerto Rico comes after residents on the island experienced an average of 36 hours of power outages in 2025 that were not caused by major adverse weather, which is 19% more than the previous year, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. When severe weather is factored in, residents experienced an additional 23 hours of power interruptions.

Customers who participate in Sunrun’s Puerto Rico distributed power plant choose how much energy to share, with most contributing a small portion of their total battery capacity. This approach ensures they retain reserve power for personal backup power in the event of grid outages. Participants are financially compensated for the power they choose to share, while Sunrun generates recurring revenue by operating the distributed power plant.

#5839. Parents' Autoimmune Disease Linked to Kids' Type 1 Diabetes Risk

— Large Swedish study highlighted shared familial susceptibility

Parental autoimmune diseases were associated with an increased risk of type 1 diabetes in offspring, according to a Swedish registry cohort study.

In an analysis of nearly 1.5 million individuals, children born to mothers with autoimmune disease during pregnancy had a 57% higher risk of developing type 1 diabetes (adjusted HR 1.57, 95% CI 1.46-1.68), according to Xingbo Mo, PhD, of Karolinska Institutet in Stockholm, and colleagues. Paternal autoimmune disease before childbirth had a comparable association (adjusted HR 1.51, 95% CI 1.37-1.67).

When parents had type 1 diabetes, the magnitude of risk was higher. Maternal type 1 diabetes was linked with a more than fourfold risk increase (HR 4.51, 95% CI 3.72-5.48), whereas paternal type 1 diabetes was associated with an even higher hazard (HR 5.79, 95% CI 4.70-7.13), they reported in JAMA Pediatrics.

"A clear gradient in type 1 diabetes risk was observed according to parental type 1 diabetes status, with the highest risk among offspring with both parents affected," the authors wrote. "The largely comparable maternal and paternal associations suggest that shared familial susceptibility may play an important role in the intergenerational transmission of type 1 diabetes risk."

While maternal and paternal estimates showed no overall difference for composite autoimmune disease, researchers identified variations across specific disease categories. Paternal associations were stronger for endocrine conditions -- most notably autoimmune thyroiditis -- whereas maternal associations were stronger for ankylosing spondylitis and gastrointestinal autoimmune disorders.

"Stronger associations for endocrine autoimmune diseases, particularly autoimmune thyroiditis, are consistent with the established clustering of endocrine autoimmune disorders and their shared immune-genetic susceptibility," the researchers noted. Yet the "disease-specific heterogeneity suggests that selected conditions may also involve parent-specific or potential intrauterine influences," they added, which "support a multifactorial model of intergenerational autoimmune transmission."

In an accompanying editorial, Mikael Knip, MD, PhD, of Biomedicum Helsinki in Finland, emphasized that an "obvious" practical takeaway is that offspring of parents with autoimmune disease warrant monitoring for type 1 diabetes.

"Consensus guidelines have been published for screening and monitoring of individuals at risk for type 1 diabetes," Knip wrote, noting that while screening efforts "may be variable based on resources available," children with a familial history "represent a definite risk group for progression to clinical type 1 diabetes."

Benjamin Nwosu, MD, chief of endocrinology at Northwell Health Cohen Children's Medical Center in New York, who was not involved with the study, underscored the necessity of early detection.

"Currently, in our practice, we screen children with type 1 diabetes for autoimmune thyroid conditions and celiac disease, because it's been published that children with type 1 diabetes have higher risk for the development of celiac and autoimmune thyroid conditions," Nwosu said in a statement.

He pointed out that the authors "did not mention that 40 to 50% of the risk for type 1 diabetes is carried on what's called the major histocompatibility complex class 2 genes or loci."

"Once you know that, you know a parent who has type 1 diabetes has some possibility of passing this condition to the offspring, not in a Mendelian autosomal dominant fashion, because type 1 is caused by what's called a polygenic aggregation of genes. But the risk is higher than in unaffected parents," he said.

The researchers evaluated 1,455,645 children born in Sweden between 2001 and 2014, with follow-up extending through 2023 (median age was 15.3 years, and 51.4% were male). Overall, 6.1% of children were exposed to maternal autoimmune diseases before delivery.

After adjusting for unmeasured shared familial factors using cousin-comparison models, the maternal association remained statistically significant (adjusted HR 1.27, 95% CI 1.08-1.50), with higher risks specifically noted for maternal endocrine autoimmune disorders and maternal type 1 diabetes.

The study team noted several limitations, including the lack of register data regarding clinical disease severity, autoantibody levels, disease activity during pregnancy, or medication use. "Such factors may modify fetal immune programming and could not be evaluated in the present study," they acknowledged.

Nwosu also cautioned that the results might not fully translate globally, noting Sweden "is located in the northern latitudes, where type 1 diabetes is almost endemic."

#5838. Batteries Beat Norway’s Hydrogen Bulk Carriers on Cost in Two Modeled Routes

Norwegian shipping company GMI Group is moving ahead with four hydrogen-electric bulk carriers for coastal freight. In October 2026, PowerCell confirmed a follow-up order that brings the program to 24 marine fuel-cell units with 5.4 MW of combined installed capacity. The first two ships, rated at 4,000 deadweight tonnes, are planned for 2027, while two additional 3,000-tonne vessels are expected in 2029.

The project has real shipbuilding commitments and substantial public support. The question is whether hydrogen makes economic sense for the freight services these vessels will provide.

GMI says its design can deliver lifetime costs 9–10% below conventional ships. Its argument combines fuel cells, batteries, an efficient hull and wind assistance. Those are useful engineering features, but most are not exclusive to hydrogen propulsion. A diesel or battery-electric ship can have a similarly efficient hull and sails. The fuel and energy systems still need to be compared on equivalent terms.

I modeled two hypothetical 3,000-tonne coastal bulk services, covering 80 and 55 nautical miles, using comparable hull performance and operating requirements. Over fifteen years, hydrogen propulsion came out 50–58% more expensive than conventional diesel, even after assuming approximately €13.1 million in public vessel support was received upfront. Battery-electric alternatives were €11.64–14.13 million cheaper than the subsidized hydrogen vessels. These are scenario results, not estimates of GMI’s actual operating contracts.

The company has not published the route and commercial data needed for a direct assessment, and the model’s vessel acquisition prices remain important uncertainties. The battery alternatives were not the cheapest option under every assumption. In the central cases they cost somewhat more than diesel over fifteen years. Their advantage was the much smaller gap to conventional operation compared with hydrogen. Battery-electric propulsion also requires adequate grid connections, charging equipment and berth time, which cannot be assumed available at every Norwegian port.

Hydrogen has a different set of requirements. Renewable electricity must be converted into hydrogen, compressed, stored, delivered to the vessel and converted back to electricity in fuel cells. Those additional processes introduce energy losses and capital costs that efficient hulls and sails cannot erase. They matter particularly for short coastal voyages where a practical charging arrangement may be possible.

Norway is using substantial public funding to support the hydrogen ships. Norsk Hydrogenforum reports Enova awards totaling roughly €42.9 million for the four vessels. Additional public support has been awarded to GreenH hydrogen production projects. Announced grants are not necessarily fully paid, and a subsidy changes the allocation of costs rather than eliminating the equipment and energy required.

There may be coastal services where voyage length, available berth time or grid limitations favour hydrogen over batteries. That needs to be established through engineering and commercial comparisons, rather than inferred from the existence of a funded shipbuilding program.

Before further public commitments to compressed-hydrogen coastal freight, Norway should require credible battery-electric bids using vessel, charging and energy prices appropriate to the expected entry-into-service dates.

#5837. EV Owners Need To Lend Out Their Cars If They Want Regular People To Go Electric

Electric vehicles will probably never fully replace the internal combustion sports car, but mainstream daily drivers are living on borrowed time. It's not like anyone with no idea which wheels are powered or how many cylinders their car has cares about a missing exhaust note. But while EVs are taking off in the rest of the world, the U.S. lags behind, thanks in large part to pro-oil propaganda. People believe all sorts of myths about EVs, and I'm sorry, but short test drives won't fix it. Which means EV owners need to start acting like they have an obligation to lend friends and family their cars.

A few days in an EV won't change anyone's mind if their lifestyle doesn't match what EVs currently offer, and that's fine. But if they've been tricked by a bunch of pro-oil myths, you may find that a few days with your car is all it takes to convince them that EVs are the best thing ever. Because even an hour-long test drive doesn't show you the benefits of living with a gas station in your garage. It's the kind of thing that probably requires a three-day loan at a minimum, because they have to see how it fits into their regular lives.

Ideally, the automakers would take the lead here, but that's probably not happening anytime soon. I've discussed this idea with employees at several automakers, and so far, I don't think anyone wants to take on the cost and complexity of dealing with dealerships to make longer-term test drives happen. So without the automakers, it falls on the EV owners who want to see EVs become more popular. We need to be the ones pushing our cars on people like they're the supposed free samples that Deputy D. Diggity Dawg Dawson insisted drug dealers would force me to take.

At least anecdotally, I don't know of anything more powerful for changing minds about EVs than time spent with your butt in the seat. Most recently, a friend had to replace their beloved Mazda CX-5 after someone hit them; they asked me about EVs, and almost before I knew it, they were the proud new owners of a Hyundai Ioniq 5. So they were already open to a car that would save them money on gas, but even they quickly realized the things they were worried about weren't actually a big deal.

According to the friend, who I will call Bill, "driving them is super f—ing fun," and he did not think he "would enjoy trying to max out the mi/kWh using the regenerative braking... But [he does]." After only a few days of driving an EV, someone experiencing their first EV was already realizing how strong the oil propaganda is and how much better EVs are at things beyond saving money on gas.

An example of a borrowing experience changing minds is my brother — he borrowed my Fiat for a week while he was in the process of replacing his company truck. With three (soon to be four!) kids, he was never going to buy a two-door hatchback, but he loved being able to charge at home so much that he went out and bought a non-Fiat EV. All it took was a little time living with an electric car that he didn't even have any interest in owning, and it changed his mind about EV ownership before he'd even driven a competitive one.

I know it's scary letting other people borrow your car, and I certainly wouldn't want you handing the keys to someone you know is irresponsible. But without automaker or federal support, we're going to have to do this on our own, and the best way to get people to change their minds about EVs is to get some real time with the cars. And what better way to make that happen is there than trading cars with someone for a few days? Friends and family help each other out, after all.

If you lend your car to someone who decides they probably shouldn't buy an EV, that's fine. No harm, no foul. But just think how happy you'll be if a few days if your car convinces someone they've been wrong about EVs and should actually get one. It's pretty nice, I'm not going to lie, and definitely worth the risk of letting someone you know drive your car. They quite literally sell themselves.

#5836. A Referendum On Elon Musk And Transgender Rights — Who’d A Thunk It?

US voters rarely, if ever, get a chance to vote on someone whose name is not on the ballot, but this year is an exceptional one with Tesla CEO Elon Musk throwing millions at key races. In years past, Musk’s seal of approval would be a planet-saving badge of climate action honor for candidates seeking office. Now he’s just another highly privileged crank exercising his outsized financial power against transgender rights. Who’d a thunk it?

Coincidentally or not, Elon Musk’s highly personal vendetta against transgender rights has materialized against the backdrop of a corresponding focus in Republican Party campaign strategy, with one early hint being his “pronouns suck” message on Twitter in July of 2020.

Musk went on to buy Twitter and rename it “X” in 2022, and the rest is transphobic history.

Also coincidentally or not, the Republican Party has been hammering against human and civil rights for generations, but the razor-sharp focus on transgender persons did not bloom into full flower until 2021, after US President Donald Trump lost his first bid for re-election.

In the aftermath of Trump’s failed insurrection of January 6, the Party alighted upon transgender rights as a powerful tool in a coordinated campaign strategy aimed at ginning up the fevered emotions of voters already besotted with US President Trump’s “MAGA” propaganda during his first term in office.

In addition to working the conservative aisle of the US Supreme Court, the anti-transgender movement has focused on legislation introduced by state lawmakers (looking at you, Florida). Among the LGBTQ+ organizations tracking the bills is the organization is the Human Rights Campaign, which has identified a distinct shift in anti-transgender strategy during the 2020 campaign cycle.

All else being equal, transgender persons are an unlikely target for a national political campaign. According to one study, self-identified transgender persons over the age of 13 make up just 1% of the US population, with much of the self-reporting cohort under age 35. As for the much-ballyhooed danger of transgender-related surgery on minors, that is vanishingly rare to the point of not occurring at all according to a 2024 Harvard study. Somewhat ironically, the same study found a “substantially higher” rate of sex-affirming surgery among non-transgender minors and adults.

For that matter, Elon Musk is known to have availed himself of body-affirming treatments as an adult, but that’s a whole ‘nother can of worms.

Regardless of the numbers, the political payoff for anti-transgender activism is substantial. Prior to 2020, Republicans did not focus narrowly on transgender rights. Their attacks were a broad barrage against marriage equality for LGBTQ+ couples, as part of a relgion-centric campaign to eliminate legal and constitutional protections. Although this type of legislation continues to appear in statehouses, HRC identified a sharp rise in the number of bills specifically attacking transgender rights during the 2020 campaign cycle. The organization summarized its findings in a report last year, stating that “opponents of LGBTQ+ equality explicitly – and admittedly – began attacking transgender youth” (emphasis added).

In the report, HRC takes note of ADF (formerly Alliance Defending Freedom) and other anti-LGBTQ+ organizations serving as “bill mills,” that funnel pre-written legislation to state lawmakers in a coordinated campaign. So, if you’re wondering why gender-related health care for minors became such a hot button issue during the 2024 election cycle, alongside transgender participation in youth sports, there’s your answer.

Although some Democrats also contributed a share to the hate fest, the bulk of the coordinated anti-transgender campaign that poured out of state legislatures in 2021, and the following years, is credited to Republican lawmakers.

The anti-transgender strategy exceeded expectations in the 2024 election cycle, aided by a late-stage change in the Democratic ticket. Podcaster Joe Rogan, among other Trump-endorsing influencers, is also credited with swinging the Gen Z (ages 18-29) vote to the Republican Party, with spectacular results.

The public mood has soured since then, to say the least. Most people may or may not ever encounter a transgender person in their whole life, but they encounter Trump every time they go to fill up their car with gas.

Still, with the well known anti-transgender activist Elon Musk contributing almost half a billion dollars (and counting) to support Republican candidates in key races around the country, transgender rights are still on the ballot — and now the whole strategy is backfiring.

CleanTechnica’s Carolyn Fortuna took note of the Great Backfiring over the weekend, observing that “Musk’s blatant attempts to influence election results are getting a lot of recent analysis and condemnation.”

“US Federal Election Commission data revealed this week that Elon Musk has donated at least $445 million into Republican-aligned political action committees and groups since last year. Interestingly, it seems that Musk’s deep influence isn’t enough, and he is worried,” Fortuna explained.

“If Democrats win big on Tuesday in midterm elections, Musk insists US democracy will come to an ‘end,” she continued, citing this message on X last Friday, October 30, from Elon Musk:

“This would result in America becoming a permanent one-party state and the end of democracy in any meaningful sense of the word. All that is needed to ensure this doesn’t happen is 51 Republican senators in 2029.”

Despite Musk’s millions, the effort is having little effect in the run-up to Election Day. Take Texas, for example, where Musk has devoted his millions, and his amplified voice, working the anti-transgender message to support Ken Paxton for US Senate against the Democratic candidate James Talerico.

Don’t just take my word for it. The well known independent journalist Judd Legum is among those taking notice. “Musk is blanketing the internet with digital ads falsely accusing Democratic Senate candidates of supporting ‘taxpayer-funded sex changes for kids,’” Legum reported on September 23.

In Texas, the attack ads are just one prong of a transgender-centric attack strategy that includes raising “questions” about Talerico’s sexual identity. The Talerico campaign, for one, is having none of it. They are turning the anti-transgender strategy back on Musk. Nothing will be certain until the dust settles after election day, but so far Musk’s millions have failed to move the needle for Paxton in Texas, where according to late breaking polls Talerico leads by a slim margin.

As reported by Houston Public Media, Talerico has been regularly blasting Musk’s influence in the Texas midterms in campaign speeches, tying the world’s richest man to a Republican candidate who drags a considerable amount of scandal and corruption baggage.

As for Musk’s interest in Tesla, not to worry. Despite Elon Musk’s personal and political baggage, the iconic automotive startup continues to hold the #1 position in EV sales in the US by a wide margin. On the other hand, General Motors and Ford are rebooting their EV efforts in anticipation of a friendlier political environment next year and beyond. Other legacy automakers, including Toyota and Subaru, have also introduced new EV models to the US market this year. In addition, Rivian and other pure play EV startups are contributing to the rising competition against Tesla for EV sales in the US. Hold on to your hats…

Or is it the brand of blue jeans originally designed for rodeo wear and that are just as old? It's unusual for two brands to leverage the same name, even when they serve different categories. The main corporate concern is that one brand's failure might possibly taint the other's fortunes.

That wasn't a primary concern when we considered the 2003 Jeep Wrangler Sahara that came our way on Monday. A bit battered, but not beyond redemption, the Wrangler (Jeep, not jeans) came with a factory hardtop and a $7,500 asking price. You all mostly liked what you saw and weren't too perturbed by the price. That combo earned the Wrangler (Jeep, not jeans) a narrow but ultimately victorious 55% 'Nice Price' nod.

Not everyone knows the difference between four-wheel drive and all-wheel drive. They sound similar and interchangeable, but the terms describe distinct drivetrains, each designed for specific purposes. The Jeep we looked at yesterday was 4WD, a drivetrain that ties all four wheels together when needed through a central locking differential for low-speed maneuvering through mud and over rocks.

By contrast, today's 2001 Audi A4 Quattro Avant is permanently activated AWD and is intended not for off-roading but for more secure handling and power application in inclement weather. For Audi, at least, this drivetrain is time-tested and rally-proven. Their personalities are further differentiated by their looks: the Jeep being brutish and basic while the Audi is one of the most handsome and elegant small estates ever offered for sale.

This one, in Cactus Green with the coal mine black interior that was favored by German carmakers back in the day, comes with a clean title, 175,020 miles under its Cactus Green belt, and an extensive list of refurbishment and renewal that has left it looking like Cinderella before the ball.

Turbocharged and intercooled, the engine makes 170 horsepower and 166 pound-feet of torque. That's routed through a five-speed automatic with Tiptronic manual controls on both the lever and steering wheel for when the driver is feeling a little spicy. Naturally, as a Quattro, it sends torque to all four wheels via a central viscous diff. We'll get to more on the mechanical situation in a sec, but first, let's address the car's appearance.

Overall, this little Audi looks to be in great condition for its age and not insignificant miles. The paint still shines; there are no significant dings or dents beneath that top coat, and the headlamp lenses show only minor clouding. According to the seller, they addressed minor paint imperfections, including bumper scrapes and hatch scratches. Surprisingly, the interior is in even better shape, looking almost as-new thanks to several replacement parts and general care and cleaning. Even the comically flimsy dashboard cup holder appears to be working as originally intended.

Plenty of other work has gone into this A4's care and feeding. That included replacing several suspension components and wheel bearings, all set at factory ride height. Most importantly, the engine has received a ton of maintenance, starting with a timing belt and water pump replacement (a plus because this is an interference engine). That work continued to the exhaust, which had the catalytic converter, O2 sensor, and mounting hardware replaced. Another major update was converting the A/C from R12 to R134. New rotors and pads, plus chasing down a number of electrical gremlins, round out the major mechanical work.

In addition to all the wrenching, the ad notes that any broken or missing parts—such as the jack and emergency triangle (German car) have all been replaced. There are still a few bugs to be tracked down, including rear door security sensors and the CD player. Fortunately, the seller is throwing in a manual for future owners. Per the ad description, the car now throws no codes and is ready for the next owner "to drive it away with confidence."

For that confident drive away to happen, there's the small matter of the seller's set price of $7,450. That's almost exactly what yesterday's more rough-hewn Jeep asked, making for an interesting contrast. Naturally, these are wildly different vehicles in both design and intent, but they hail from almost the same year and, as noted, fall in the same price range. Which would you rather have?

Wait. Strike that. Let's focus on the Audi for now. We do, after all, have to consider it on its own merits, not in comparison to a truck or a pair of blue jeans, whichever yesterday's Wrangler was.

With that in mind, what's your take on this well-cared-for and rehabilitated A4 Avant at that $7,450 asking price? Does that feel fair given its now turnkey presentation? Or is that too much for a car that's already nickel-and-dimed its present owner significantly?

#5834. CTE in NFL Players: What a New Study Tells Us -- And What It Doesn't

— Does the new research mean 3 in 4 football players are at risk?

A statistical model that extrapolated data from deceased National Football League (NFL) brain donors to include all former NFL players who died from 2008 through 2023 estimated that nearly three in four had chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).

Yorghos Tripodis, PhD, of the Boston University School of Public Health, and colleagues developed the model by quantifying cognitive symptoms of NFL brain donors who had CTE assessments. CTE can be identified only through autopsy.

After adjusting for bias associated with brain donation, the model estimated the prevalence of CTE at death was 74.5% (95% CI 69.6-78.3) for all former NFL players who died from 2008 through 2023, Tripodis and colleagues reported in JAMA Network Open.

The analysis incorporated a selection ratio to estimate the prevalence of CTE. The ratio assumed that brain donation was driven primarily by family members observing cognitive symptoms in former NFL players.

"This is an interesting attempt to statistically account for the problem of selective donation into a brain bank so that they can estimate the prevalence of CTE among all NFL players who died during the time interval they were looking at when they only could analyze a subset of them," observed Marc Weisskopf, PhD, ScD, of the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health in Boston, who wasn't involved with the study.

The numbers don't necessarily apply to all NFL players, he pointed out. "The deaths they are working with are about 10% of all that could have occurred in that period, and there are reasons to suspect CTE would be less common among the still-living players when they eventually die," Weisskopf told MedPage Today.

"The statistical approach is sound, although it's important to realize that it is very dependent on some assumptions -- notably that brain donation is entirely driven by cognitive symptoms and that those are captured by dementia on the death certificate and their adjustment for additional mild cognitive impairment," he said.

CTE has four distinct stages, with higher CTE stages correlating with more severe cognitive symptoms. "Even if we were able to determine an unbiased estimate of the proportion of living and deceased players with CTE, we still don't have information on their probable CTE stage, which has the most meaning for their everyday lives and health," noted Rachel Grashow, PhD, MS, also of Harvard, who also wasn't involved with the study.

The study findings do not apply to other groups, observed Julie Stamm, PhD, of the University of Wisconsin-Madison, who wasn't part of the study. "It does not provide an estimate of CTE among athletes in other sports or at lower levels of play," Stamm told MedPage Today.

"Greater lifetime repetitive head impact exposure has been linked to an increased risk of developing CTE, so it is likely that the prevalence would be higher among NFL players than those who played at lower levels," she added. "However, we cannot estimate the prevalence among players at lower levels at this time."

Tripodis and colleagues used UNITE brain bank data and national death index records to evaluate former NFL players who died from 2008 through 2023. The mean duration of play was 5.1 years and 41.1% of deceased players were ages 80 or older when they died.

Of 2,362 deceased former NFL players, 396 were brain donors and 1,966 were nondonors. Of 387 donors, 362 (93.5%) had CTE at autopsy. The estimated prevalence of all-cause dementia was 27.2% (95% CI 22.6-31.6).

The median selection ratio was 4.97 (95% CI 4.72-5.26), meaning that former players with cognitive symptoms were five times more likely to have their brains donated by their family than those without these symptoms.

"The findings of this cross-sectional study suggest that selection bias materially inflates donor-based prevalence estimates but is unlikely to fully explain the high burden of CTE neuropathology among this population," Tripodis and co-authors stated.

Studies like this can refocus attention to the "20,000 living former NFL players, some of whom are suffering with cognitive symptoms or have been diagnosed with dementia," Grashow told MedPage Today. The Football Players Health Study at Harvard has more than 5,000 former players in its cohort, she noted.

"In our conversations with and ongoing study of these NFL players, we've found that head injury increases risk for treatable conditions that -- if left untreated -- increases risk for cognitive issues and dementia. These include sleep apnea, high blood pressure, low testosterone, depression, anxiety, tinnitus, and more," she added.

"So, if we are thinking about how these recent findings relate to the many thousands of former living players, the story shifts to one of surveilling and treating former players for treatable conditions so we can reduce their dementia and heart disease risk," Grashow said. "This, we believe, is one of the best ways we can tackle the potential symptoms, risks, and challenges of CTE right now -- before we turn to estimating prevalence, which is at the end of life."

#5832. Hyundai's XRT Off-Road Division Is On The Right Path But A Step Behind

There's nothing more in vogue right now than automakers soft-roader-ing their crossovers for weekend warrior types who enjoy a bit of camping or a dirt road every once in a while. Honda has TrailSport, Subaru has Wilderness, Toyota has TRD, GMC has AT4, and so on and so forth. Of course one of the largest automakers in the U.S. would want to get in on the action, so Hyundai spun up its own off-road sub-brand a few years back: XRT, which stands for Extreme Rugged Terrain.

What started out as more of a trim and appearance package on vehicles like the first-gen Palisade and fourth-gen Tucson and Santa Fe has evolved into offering styling changes with a bit of added capability when the going gets bumpy. With the introduction of Hyundai's XRT Pro trim on the Palisade and upcoming fifth-gen Tucson, that idea gets taken up another notch. However, after spending a day with both the 2026 Santa Fe XRT and 2026 Palisade XRT Pro off-roading in rural Missouri, I'm not totally sure Hyundai is all the way there yet. That's not to say the Korean automaker isn't on the right path and won't keep improving expeditiously, but as it stands right now, it may be just a step or two behind.

Full Disclosure: Hyundai flew me out to Bentonville, Arkansas, put me up in a very nice hotel and fed me, all so I could sample the 2026 Santa Fe XRT and 2026 Palisade XRT Pro.

It can be sort of tricky to evaluate the capability of a soft-roader like Hyundai's XRT fleet. Technically, both the Palisade XRT Pro and Santa Fe XRT were able to do everything that was thrown at them on this program, but they both lacked a bit of the sure-footedness I just experienced in Honda's Passport TrailSport, and that was on a far more technical and challenging course. That being said, what I did with the XRT siblings is probably 10 times as grueling as what the average Hyundai owner will do with their SUVs. There's also the issue of tires. While the Passport TrailSport is fitted with beefy General Grabber A/T Sport all-terrain rubber, the Santa Fe XRT makes do with less-aggressive Continental TerrainContact A/Ts, which leads to a good bit of wheel slippage.

Still, both XRTs do an admirable job of tackling trails, though rock crawlers they are not. The Palisade XRT Pro I drove was certainly the more capable of the two, thanks to its electronic limited-slip differential in the rear and a 360-degree camera that helped overcome its sheer size, but it never felt particularly at home, even if it did tackle every obstacle without much protest.

I say much protest because, while the car didn't get stuck at any point, the 4,575-pound crossover didn't exactly seem happy, and that especially goes for its Hyundai-built 8-speed transmission. While the naturally aspirated 3.5-liter V6 provided enough power (287 horsepower and 260 pound-feet of torque) to get up just about anything despite a lack of low-end oomph, I could tell that the 8-speed was none too pleased. I couldn't hear it on the road, but when switching to the Sand setting in its Trail drive mode, there was a noticeable whine coming from it on the throttle. A temperature readout in the gauge cluster also served as a constant reminder it was, uh, hot, and when I got out of the car, there was an unmistakable smell of hot transmission wafting through the air. From a functional standpoint, the XRT Pro didn't skip a beat, which is certainly a testament to the rest of the Palisade's drivetrain and its 8.4 inches of ground clearance; it bottomed out far less than I expected it to.

It's a similar story with the Santa Fe XRT. It may lack the e-LSD and all-out grunt of the Palisade, but it does make up for that somewhat with more low-end grunt courtesy of a torquey turbocharged 2.5-liter inline-4 that pumps out 277 hp and 311 lb-ft of torque. This drivetrain lent itself far better to the old-school way of getting yourself unstuck: give 'er some gas. Sure, there are 10 fewer horses than the Palisade's V6, but an extra 51 torques is massive.

Still, you can tell the Santa Fe is a far less luxury-oriented product than the Palisade, and I got bumped around a hell of a lot more than I did in the Palisade. Obviously, there's a price delta to consider, as the Santa Fe XRT starts at $43,940 including destination, and the Palisade XRT Pro has a far more costly $51,820 entrance price.

Currently, there are four XRT models on sale: the two I've been talking about, and then the Santa Cruz XRT and the Ioniq 5 XRT. I've driven the Ioniq and had a pretty good time with it, but came away feeling it was more of a styling exercise than anything else. Sure, it can handle some dirt, but that's just about it. While all these models do come with all-terrain tires, a bit more ground clearance, upped towing capacity, better approach and departure angles, and functional front recovery hooks, they're without a doubt behind industry frontrunners like Honda TrailSport and Subaru Wilderness when it comes to real capability.

I believe that's because XRT, as a brand, is so new. Hyundai's still trying to find its footing in an ever-more crowded world. It promises that its next product, based on the fifth-generation Tucson, will be its best yet, and far more than an appearance package. Even though the Tucson won't have the e-LSD of the Palisade XRT Pro, despite sharing the "Pro" moniker, it will have skid plates, all-terrain tires, 8.3 inches of ground clearance, some sick body cladding, and Hyundai's new off-road software called Smart Terrain Assist.

That program has the ability to analyze the terrain ahead of you, determining traction and slip conditions. From there, it provides visual guidance via green, orange or red "stuck zones," and shows the driver the best route to take. It works in concert with Automatic Terrain Detection (which has auto, snow, mud, sand and rock modes) with intelligent mode switching to remove any guesswork from off-roading. Clearly, Hyundai wants to make it as friendly to first-time off-roaders as possible.

Lest we forget, this same team is working on the body-on-frame Hyundai Boulder SUV, which will likely be powered by a hybrid or EREV drivetrain. It shares underpinnings with a future body-on-frame truck Hyundai is also working on, and it's targeted specifically at the American market.

While I'm not sure Hyundai's XRT division is quite the cream of the crop just yet when it comes to soft-roading — it might be a bit too focused on aesthetics, rather than actual performance — there's little doubt in my mind that it'll get to the front of the pack sooner rather than later. Just look at what this massive company has done with its N performance division, or what it has done with Genesis when it comes to luxury. When Hyundai puts its mind to something, it gets the job done, and I don't expect XRT to be any different.

#5831. Jackery Launches Explorer 100D Portable Power Station. Maximum Capability For Carryon Compatibility

Jackery just launched the Explorer 100D portable power station. This is Jackery’s smallest battery, giving a new level of versatility to power many of the devices people rely on most. Meanwhile, it integrates  the durability and safety people expect from Jackery’s larger models into a compact case.

The Explorer 100D has a capacity of 96 Wh (30,000mAh) which puts it just below the carryon limit for domestic and international flights. Meanwhile, up to 158 W of output is more than enough to charge a laptop. The 100D is compatible with advanced protocols including AVS, PD 3.1 and PPS, providing precise charging, particularly for Apple products.

The Explorer 100D measures 4.6” X 3.4” X 3.4”(11.6 X  8.3 cm X  8.5 cm), or about the size of a softball. It weighs 1.87 lbs. (850 g). This is a bit larger than the typical power bank, but much smaller than the typical solar generator. It is also smaller and lighter than the Explorer 100 Plus that it replaces, while also increasing in power output.

On the test sample model, I found the form factor very convenient. It is not small enough to fit in your pants pocket, but the rectangular case with rounded corners was easy to fit in a backpack or carryon bag. A cloth handle makes it easy to hold, and a shoulder strap is available. I had a credentials lanyard from a previous media event on hand, and it worked fine as a strap for the lightweight battery.

On the front of the battery are two 140 W USB-C ports and an 18 W USB-A port. The left USB-C port can both charge the battery and discharge to another device. The battery can also be discharged through the other two ports while it charges. The battery does not come with a charger, although a USB-C cable is provided. I was able to charge the Explorer 100D on a wide range of chargers, although lower powered chargers take a while to charge the large capacity battery.

The front display default shows battery charge percentage as well as input and output power. However, you can switch the display to also show power output to each port or battery health, cycles and temperature.

Unlike some of Jackery’s larger batteries, the 100D does not have cooling fans or vents in the case. The LFP battery is rated for 3000 full charge cycles, good for 8 years of daily use. This is far more durable than many Li-ion power banks, which commonly only offer a few hundred charge cycles. It is also a 50% improvement over the previous Explorer 100 Plus model that it replaces. Of note, while this model does comply with China’s strict CCC (China Compulsory Certification), the logo was not printed on the test model I received, although that may change in the future. Without the logo present, it could be taken away if travelling in China. However, the battery did have FCC and SGS certification printed on it, which are more relevant to most US customers.

The portable battery can function as a solar generator by accepting direct solar input up to 100 W. This makes it a bit different than many power banks. Solar panels connect through the USB-C charge port. which may require the purchase of an adaptor, depending on the panel used. Jackery’s lightweight, folding SolarSaga 100 Air could charge the battery in less than two hours. The battery can also take 12 V or 24V input from a car, boat or RV. Using a traditional USB-C charger, the Explorer 100D can accept up to 140 W of input power.

The Explorer 100D  test model came with 30% charge and reached a full charge in about an hour. While the battery was charging, I was able to charge my phone and another power bank off the output ports while the battery was charging. I initially charged the battery off the HomePower 1000 Plus V2, which has a 140 W USB-C output. With similar styling, it looked like a baby of the larger battery when placed on top. Of course, the battery would take longer to charge on lower power. However, it could be used to accumulate charge over time and discharge more quickly for a device like a laptop that needs more power than what may be available from a charge jack at a hotel room or airport.

While the battery will often be used to charge phones, the Explorer 100D ran my T-Mobile Wi-Fi router all day, with capacity left to charge my phone and tablet. When used with a laptop with a USB-C charge port, the small battery could power a remote office.

I was also able to run a small personal fan off of the Explorer 100D. With peak power draw at 5 watts, it didn’t pose much of a challenge for the battery. This would come in handy at an outdoor event or while fishing on a hot day.

On Halloween, I used the battery to power an old Bluetooth speaker for hours of handing out treats, while keeping our phones charged. The black and orange design fits well with the holiday decorations. By the end of the night, the battery still had over 90% capacity.

I also used the battery on a trip to an apple harvest festival. While charging ports were in short supply in the car, the Explorer 100D kept phone and camera batteries topped up. The rubber feet kept the battery from shifting around when placed on the center console.

The Jackery Explorer 100D launches as a two-unit bundle for $179.99 at select Costco warehouse locations from the start of November 2026. Individual units will then become available at Walmart for $99 on November 15th, just in time for holiday travel.

Frost & Sullivan recently named Jackery the World’s No.1 Solar Generator Brand. Jackery leads in solar generator sales volume globally and has pioneered multiple innovations in portable power. The Explorer 100D is the latest example. The company has a focus on providing solutions for customer needs with durable products that have exceeded my expectations in testing. After trying the Explorer 100D, I also find it to be more useful than I originally expected, using it in a wide range of applications. While the Explorer 100D clearly is not going to solve all of the world’s energy problems, it provides another power option that meets the needs of many customers while integrating well with Jackery’s expanding range of solar and energy storage products. As Steven Wang, CEO of Jackery Americas puts it:

Power support is often most effective when it’s highly portable and backed by comprehensive compatibility and a long lifespan. Developed for peak productivity, the Explorer 100D represents years of honed design and feature implementation, while maintaining focus on the top-quality engineering and unmatched consistency that make Jackery portable power stations must-haves for work and travel. Thanks to that collection of refined expertise, it’s among the longest-lasting ultra-portable batteries ever.

I look forward to putting the Explorer 100D to the test during some upcoming travel over the next few months. I also look forward to seeing what Jackery comes up with next in versatile, portable power.

#5830. Washington State Resident Dies From Bird Flu Following Exposure to Infected Cattle

— Two other U.S. deaths have been tied to bird flu since 2024

A person in Washington state has died from complications of the bird flu, the first such U.S. death in a year.

The Yakima County resident, who had previous health conditions, was exposed to avian influenza at a dairy with infected cattle and had been hospitalized. The person died Sunday, county health officials said.

Two other U.S. deaths have been tied to bird flu since it became a national public health concern in 2024. The first, announced in January 2025, was an elderly person in Louisiana who had a version of bird flu known as H5N1. The other, in Washington state, died in November 2025 from a rarer version called H5N5.

Yakima County officials did not release any additional details about the person who recently died. The CDC said the person was infected with H5N1.

County officials have reported that 33 dairy herds recently have tested positive for H5N1.

They say three human infections have been linked to exposure at a dairy, and that the Yakima Health District is working with the state health department to find people who were in close contact with those people and monitor them for symptoms.

The H5N1 bird flu has been spreading widely among wild birds, poultry, cows, and other animals for several years. Health concerns escalated in early 2024 when infections spread among U.S. livestock. Its presence in the environment increases the chances that people will be exposed, and potentially catch it, officials have said.

More than 70 human infections have been reported in the U.S. since the beginning of 2024, according to the CDC. But there is no known person-to-person spread and the risk to the general public is low, the agency says.

The agency analyzed the genetic sequence of the virus from the person who died in Washington and found no changes that would make the virus spread more easily or cause more severe illness, a CDC spokesperson said Monday.

Officials continue to urge people who have contact with sick or dead birds to take precautions, including wearing respiratory and eye protection and gloves when handling poultry. People who work on farms are considered to be at higher risk.

#5828. Germany’s Hydrogen Pipeline Reached Marl. Its Market Still Needs to Add Up.

Germany’s hydrogen backbone achieved a genuine milestone on August 4, 2026. RWE and its partners announced that renewable hydrogen produced during commissioning at Lingen had reached Marl Chemical Park, roughly 120 kilometres away. Electrolysers, converted natural gas pipelines and industrial receiving infrastructure were working together.

The GET H2 consortium deserves credit for getting the equipment operating. But completing a hydrogen pipeline and establishing an economically competitive market for the hydrogen moving through it are different achievements.

The announcement did not disclose the quantity received at Marl, the price paid by an industrial customer or which existing hydrogen production was displaced. The English release describes hydrogen being available for industrial use, while the German release says it was used. Neither provides the industrial mass balance needed to determine the actual emissions benefit. The network also contained hydrogen from earlier commissioning activities, which makes tracing individual molecules through the pipeline less useful than measuring what changed at the receiving industrial facilities.

Marl is hardly a new hydrogen customer. The chemical park has used hydrogen for decades in integrated production processes. Providing another source may be useful, especially where renewable hydrogen replaces fossil-derived supply, but existing demand does not automatically become commercially viable demand for a considerably more expensive feedstock.

The larger infrastructure ambition makes that distinction important. Germany’s approved hydrogen core network covers 9,040 kilometres and has expected investment costs of €18.9 billion. Much of the network will use converted natural gas pipelines. These are approved plans and anticipated investments, not evidence that the entire network has been built or that future customers have committed to using it.

There are genuine industrial commitments. RWE has a 15-year agreement with TotalEnergies to supply approximately 30,000 tonnes of renewable hydrogen annually to the Leuna refinery from 2030. That provides a named customer, volume and contract period. The price is undisclosed, and European fuel regulations help create demand for renewable hydrogen in refining.

That is a much stronger commercial signal than commissioning a pipeline. The question is how many comparable customers exist, what they can afford and whether their businesses will continue using hydrogen over the decades required to recover infrastructure investments.

The wider European outlook has become less optimistic. ENTSOG’s October 2026 draft assessment reduced its 2030 hydrogen demand assumption from 620 TWh to 335 TWh, a 46% reduction from its 2024 assessment. Its 2040 assumption fell 33%, from 1,929 TWh to 1,296 TWh. These are changes to European planning scenarios, not measurements of declining actual hydrogen consumption, but they matter when infrastructure economics depend on demand growth.

My central model of hydrogen supplied through the Lingen system produces an illustrative delivered cost of about €9.06/kg after assumed capital support, compared with a €3/kg conventional hydrogen benchmark. Those are scenario values, not RWE’s actual costs or the undisclosed price paid at Marl. The gap illustrates the challenge facing industrial manufacturers selling chemicals into competitive international markets.

Hydrogen remains an important industrial feedstock. Well-located connections between producers and customers with durable demand may be worthwhile. Germany needs evidence that the customers and products can support the investment, rather than assuming that building enough pipelines will bring the market into existence.

#5826. Late-Stage Sickle Cell Disease Study Splits on Main Goals

— Mitapivat improved hemoglobin response, but no significant benefit for pain crises

The thalassemia drug mitapivat (Aqvesme) significantly improved hemoglobin response in patients with sickle cell disease but failed to top placebo when it came to reducing pain crises in a phase III trial that aims to support an expanded approval.

In the RISE UP trial, 41% of patients assigned to the oral pyruvate kinase activator had a hemoglobin response, as compared with 3% of placebo recipients (P<0.0001). But that didn't translate into a reduction in the annualized rate of sickle cell pain crises (2.6 for mitapivat vs 3.1 for placebo, P=0.1213), reported researchers led by Biree Andemariam, MD, of the New England Sickle Cell Institute at University of Connecticut Health in Farmington.

Beyond those two primary endpoints, treatment with mitapivat was associated with improved markers of hemolysis, reduced transfusion burden, and additional clinical benefits in the subset of patients with a hemoglobin response, but not with improvements in patient-reported fatigue, the study authors wrote in The Lancet.

These mitapivat data, which are currently under review with the FDA, arrive amid turbulence in the drug market for sickle cell disease. Crizanlizumab (Adakveo), approved in 2019, lost its marketing authorization in Europe after randomized trial data showed the drug failed to top placebo when it came to vaso-occlusive crises, though it's still available in the U.S.

And voxelotor (Oxbryta), which was granted accelerated approval, also in 2019, was pulled from global markets after trial data turned up an imbalance in deaths and acute vaso-occlusive crises for patients on the hemoglobin S polymerization inhibitor.

Mitapivat is currently approved as a disease-modifying treatment for anemia in adults with alpha- or beta-thalassemia, and an approval decision in sickle cell disease is expected by February of next year.

Labeling for mitapivat includes a boxed warning due to the risk of liver injury, which also warranted a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy (REMS) program. The FDA has requested an analysis on whether a REMS would be needed in sickle cell disease, but drugmaker Agios Pharmaceuticals said the data so far have shown no cases of liver injury that follow the pattern or severity seen in the thalassemia trials.

The RISE UP trial was conducted across 69 sites in 15 countries and randomized 207 patients older than 16 years with anemia and recurrent sickle cell pain crises in a 2:1 ratio to twice-daily mitapivat (100 mg) or placebo.

At baseline, participants had a median age of 25 years, 57.5% were female, mean hemoglobin was about 8.5 g/dL, and they averaged 3.4 sickle cell pain crises per year.

The primary endpoint of hemoglobin response was defined as a 1 g/dL or greater increase in average hemoglobin concentration from week 24 to week 52 compared with the baseline.

In a commentary accompanying the study, Jennifer Knight-Madden, MBBS, PhD, and Zachary Ramsay, MBBS, both of the University of the West Indies in Kingston, Jamaica, noted that despite the mixed results on the primary endpoints, "there could be clinical benefit" among the mitapivat responders.

The findings should be interpreted with caution, they noted, but post-hoc analyses suggested the mitapivat-treated participants "who achieved a hemoglobin response experienced lower annualized rates of sickle cell pain crises, fewer related hospitalizations and emergency department visits, longer times to first and second sickle cell pain crises, and lower fatigue scores compared with non-responders."

"The findings provide evidence that a clinically meaningful benefit can exist within a subset of patients," they wrote. "As acknowledged by the authors, this study was not designed to identify patients likely to achieve a hemoglobin response, and differences in hemoglobin response could be due to genetic and epigenetic modifiers, red cell metabolic differences, and co-inherited red cell variants."

As for safety data, mitapivat was associated with lower rates of grade ≥3 adverse events (AEs), at 33% versus 41% with placebo, and lower rates of serious AEs (20% vs 29%), Andemariam and colleagues reported. One of the serious AEs in a mitapivat-treated patient was considered treatment-related, however.

Overall, AEs leading to treatment discontinuation occurred in 4% of patients in the mitapivat group and in 3% of the placebo group. Despite no signal of liver injury in the study, some hepatic-related AEs did lead to mitapivat discontinuation, including one patient with increases in aspartate aminotransferase (grade 3) and bilirubin (grade 2), another patient with hepatic enzyme increases (grade 4) deemed unrelated to treatment, a patient with hepatic cytolysis (grade 2) and other AEs, and one patient with transaminase increases (grade 2) considered secondary to an infection.

Deaths occurred in 2% of the mitapivat arm and 3% of the placebo arm, with none deemed treatment-related.

#5825. Swarm Of Electric Trucks Coming To US (Battery Swapping Included?)

Tesla CEO Elon Musk famously ditched the idea of EV battery swapping back in 2015 after a brief experiment. That pretty much laid the idea to rest here in the US, but other EV stakeholders soldiered on. The latest example is the Australian firm Janus Electric, which is bringing its Class 8 heavy duty electric truck conversions to North America. Janus offers a battery-as-a-service model that includes both charging and swapping…so, is battery swapping finally coming here to the US?.

Battery swapping for two-wheelers and larger EVs is commonplace in some overseas markets, with industry leader Nio being one example. So far, though, swapping stations for e-bikes are the only sign of emerging activity in the US.

Musk’s opinion aside, a modern battery swapping station can change a spent electric car battery for a fresh one in just a few minutes, or less time than it takes to drive through an automated car wash. On the other hand, considering today’s EV fast charging technology, battery swapping is somewhat less relevant to passenger cars and other light duty vehicles. Access to home charging is another factor that can limit the appeal of driving to a battery swapping station for a refresh.

Electric trucks, though, are another kettle of fish. Every minute counts in the fast paced transportation industry. Waiting in line for an EV charging station to free up is a non-starter, and then there’s the charging time. Even the much-heralded Tesla Semi Class 8 truck can take hours to reach a full charge overnight, though the truck is reported to achieve 60-70% charge in as little as 30-45 minutes at fast charging stations.

The time factor explains why battery swapping for trucks is appearing in overseas markets. The seeds of change have also begun to sprout up in the US, where the the diesel-to-electric conversion field is beginning to offer some opportunities. Last summer, for example, the US startup Revoy (formerly SixWheels) announced a swappable battery retrofit for Class 8 diesel trucks. The retrofit consists of a battery unit inserted between the cab and the trailer, which can be swapped out in a matter of minutes. The unit does not replace the engine, but it reportedly cuts diesel emissions by up to 85%, with a 95% fuel savings aided by regenerative braking.

The US Army is also dipping a toe in the conversion field with “idling kits,” which are batteries powerful enough to run on-board equipment for military vehicles in near silence, without the giveaway noise and heat signature involved in idling the vehicle’s engine. No word yet on whether or not swap-outs will be part of the picture, but the technology pieces are in place.

So much for the current state of affairs. Last week a full diesel-to-electric conversion opportunity suddenly appeared when the Canadian lithium-ion battery specialist Electrovaya announced a new $26 million diesel-to-electric supply agreement with the Janus that leverages Electrovaya’s proprietary “Infinity Battery Technology, a durable system compatible with daily swapping cycles for Class 8 trucks.

The $26 million agreement represents just the initial phase of orders for the US and Canadian markets. “Electrovaya has also agreed to invest approximately $1.4 million in Janus for up to 4.2 million shares, together with up to 6.3 million warrants,” Electrovaya noted, indicating a long term partnership allowing plenty of room for scaleup.

“Janus’s approach converts existing diesel prime movers to battery-electric operation and pairs them with swappable battery packs and Janus Charge & Change Stations, allowing fleets to exchange batteries in minutes rather than wait hours to recharge, and to electrify without the capital cost of purchasing new trucks,” Electrovaya explained (see additional coverage on CleanTechnica  here and here).

Janus’s footprint in North American is still tiny, at 118 truck conversion orders and commitments in the US and Canada combined. However, the firm’s business with Electrovaya should help ramp up the activity. Janus has already begun deliveries to Electrovaya, and Electrovaya has announced a major expansion of its North American manufacturing footprint. The showpiece is a production facility in Jamestown, New York covering lithium-ion battery cells, modules, and packs.  Start of operations is schedule for sometime next year.

With US President Donald Trump’s war in Iran continuing to elevate diesel costs, both Janus Electric and Electrovaya smell an end to the partisan war on EVs that rocked the US market after Trump took office in January of 2025. “Electrovaya’s expanding North American manufacturing capabilities will be important as we scale,” said Janus CEO and Managing Director Ben Hutt in a press statement.

“The investment is a strong vote of confidence in our technology and approach to electrifying heavy transport,” Hutt added.

The CEO of Electrovaya, Dr. Raj Das Gupta, also underscored the potential for rapid scaleup. “Janus has developed a practical solution to one of the major challenges facing heavy transport, enabling diesel-powered trucks to be converted to electric without compromising their commercial operations,” Gupta emphasized.

“Our strategic investment, together with the warrants, aligns us closely with Janus’s long-term growth,” Gupta also explained, with warrants referring to up to 6.3 million in contracts for future stock transactions.

If you’re wondering how much traction Electrovaya and Janus will gain in the US electric truck conversion space, that’s a good question considering Trump’s on-again, off-again trade wars with the upstairs neighbors.

The factory in New York State should help push matters along. As if on cue, over the weekend the White House also signaled that Trump is suddenly willing to call off his tariff dogs, potentially leading to a trade deal with Canda that could help accelerate activity in the US electric truck conversion field, among other areas.

On the other hand, the negotiations are described as achieving an early stage “concept” of a deal, which makes it seem more like a weak effort to gin up voter support for the Republican ticket ahead of Election Day on November 3. The concept of a deal could just as easily de-materialize by the morning of November 4.

Deal or no deal, Trump is scheduled to leave office in January of 2029 at the latest — peacefully this time, one hopes — opening up space for a new era of stability and mutual benefit in US-Canada trade relations.

In the meantime, keep an eye on Electrovaya for more activity in the electrification field, with or without help from the US market. In addition to supplying batteries for electric truck conversion, the company anticipates business in the fields of material handling, robotics, defense, and AI data center infrastructure.

Photo: The Australian firm Janus Electric has hooked up with Canada’s Electrovaya to accelerate the electric truck conversion field in North America, regardless of the sharp U-turn in US electrification policy (cropped, courtesy of Janus).

#5824. These Are The Cars You'd Lease But Never Buy

To lease, or not to lease? That is the question millions of Americans face every single year when it comes time to take home a new vehicle. I wanted to know what car you'd definitely lease but would never buy. What car would you happily have in your driveway for two or three years, racking up repair and deprecation costs on the automaker's dime, all just to give it back in 36 months? Of course, you can't get attached to these vehicles, because your time with them is going to be finite, so the emotional folks among us may not like the idea of leasing, and neither will those of us who like to keep cars for years and years.

In any case, why don't you drop on down below and check out what cars your fellow Jalops would consider leasing but would never buy? Did you buy one of the cars on this list? What's it like feeling like a fool in front of everyone?

Oh! Really quick, to everyone who took the time to say they'd never lease a car: shame on you. That wasn't the question, and I don't care. That's why I made a shame slide for the rest of us — folks who are willing to participate in polite society — to gawk at you all. Boo, you!

Anything German. Under lease, I'm protected by free repairs when inevitably something breaks. My pockets aren't deep enough to keep the car running post warranty expiration if it were a purchase or I bought out the lease.

I have this irrational love of the Land Rover Defender. Can't explain why. At least it can be treated like the Land Rover safari vehicles of not long ago. But there is a zero chance I'd ever hang onto one for more than five years, so it's a lease. Insert Land Rover quality stereotype here, but the list of electrical gremlins they suffer is legion. And they don't improve with age. But for that three year lease, I'd beat the snot out of it and buff out any scratches from trees and shrubs at turn-in time.

Land Rover Defender. Why? because not reliable and expensive to maintain. But for the fun and the driving experience.

I wouldn't worry about software/tech being outdated as long as the driving experience is sublime.

Land Rovers. There is no universe in which they're reliable, but damn if they aren't desirable. The cabins are beautiful, they're butter-smooth, and they still have some great off-roading chops, but there's no way I'd want to spend more than a few years with one.

Simple literally ANY EV, they only make sense to lease or buy outright. IF you get financing you would be very under water very fast considering their rate of depreciation.
